 Daylight saving time ends November 1 in most of the U.S.
 How Daylight Saving Time Affects U.S. Businesses
 by 
 The FINANCIAL 
 October 25, 2026 
 in 
 America 
 Reading Time: 5 mins read
 8 
 0 
 A 
 A 
 A 
 A 
 Reset 
 0 
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 
 Daylight saving time ends November 1 across most of the United States, with clocks moving back one hour at 2 a.m. local time. The change is one week away as of Sunday, October 25.
 The U.S. Naval Observatory’s 2026 calendar confirms the November date. The transition is tied to local time rather than a single nationwide instant, so it takes place at different moments across the country’s time zones.
 At the changeover, 2 a.m. becomes 1 a.m., repeating an hour. The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s current rules put the 2026 daylight saving period between March 8 and November 1.
 Where clocks will not change
 Hawaii and most of Arizona do not observe daylight saving time; the Navajo Indian Reservation is an exception within Arizona. Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa and the U.S. Virgin Islands also do not observe it.
 The shift returns observing areas to standard time. It changes the clock reading associated with daylight, rather than adding daylight to the day.

 What states can change
 Under the Department of Transportation’s explanation of federal law , states may exempt themselves from daylight saving time. They cannot independently adopt permanent daylight saving time.
 States that observe the seasonal system must follow the federally mandated start and end dates. DOT oversees uniform observance and time-zone boundaries, but says it does not have authority to repeal or change daylight saving time.
 The federal framework dates to the Uniform Time Act of 1966. Federal oversight of time zones began earlier, under the Standard Time Act of 1918, and passed to DOT when the department was created in 1966.
 The American system is not universal. A 2023 international overview published by The FINANCIAL examined how seasonal clock changes differ across countries.
 Questions and answers
 When does daylight saving time end in 2026?
 November 1 at 2 a.m. local time in observing U.S. areas.
 Do clocks move forward or backward?
 Backward one hour, from 2 a.m. to 1 a.m.
 Does every state observe it?
 No. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not.
 Can states adopt permanent daylight saving time themselves?
 No, under DOT’s explanation of current federal law.
 Did U.S. clocks change on October 25?
 No. The scheduled U.S. fall transition is November 1.
 How Daylight Saving Time Affects U.S. Businesses 
 When daylight saving time ends on November 1, U.S. businesses operating overnight will face an immediate expense: an additional hour of work for employees whose shifts span the clock change. Retailers will lose an hour of evening daylight, while managers will need to check schedules, payroll systems and staffing.
 Daylight saving time and consumer spending 
 One of the most detailed U.S. studies of spending around clock changes came from the JPMorgan Chase Institute, which examined anonymized credit and debit card transactions from October 2012 through June 2015.
 Its 2016 report compared Los Angeles, which changes its clocks, with Phoenix, which does not. Daily card spending per capita in Los Angeles increased 0.9 percent relative to Phoenix during the 30 days after the spring transition. After the fall transition, it declined 3.5 percent.
 More than two-thirds of the fall decline came from fewer transactions rather than smaller purchases. Spending on goods fell more than spending on services, and the decline was greater during the workweek than on weekends.
 For retailers, a practical response is to examine transactions by hour before changing opening times. If purchases move earlier after the clock change, staffing, collection appointments and promotions can follow that pattern. Testing an earlier offer against an evening offer would provide a firmer basis for decisions than assuming customers will stop shopping after dark.
 Restaurants and service businesses should examine their own booking records separately. In the institute’s study, their spending patterns were less sensitive to the fall transition than those of merchants selling goods.

 Research on productivity has concentrated heavily on the spring change. 
 A 2009 study in the Journal of Applied Psychology examined U.S. mining injuries from 1983 through 2006. Researchers Christopher Barnes and David Wagner found more injuries, and injuries of greater severity, on Mondays immediately after the spring transition.
 A separate analysis of federal time-use data found that workers slept an average of 40 minutes less on those Mondays. The researchers did not find significant changes in sleep, injury frequency or injury severity after the autumn transition.
 More recent work has examined digital activity. A 2024 study published in the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization used GitHub activity to investigate the spring transition. Daily activity declined for about two days, while reductions during early working hours extended into a second week.
 Employers can prepare by avoiding unnecessary early starts, reviewing overtime schedules and allowing flexibility where operations permit. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends raising awareness of the spring transition’s risks and considering reductions in critical or physically and mentally demanding tasks while workers adjust.
 Workplace safety findings differ 
 The autumn change also warrants attention, although research does not produce a uniform account of injury risk.
 A study published in December 2025 analyzed timestamps for 738,828 reported U.S. workplace injuries in 2023. Researchers found an increase associated with the fall clock change, while the spring change did not produce a statistically significant effect. The authors described the analysis as an initial demonstration of the new reporting dataset’s research potential.
 Its findings differ from the older mining study, which covered another workforce and period.
 Payroll needs the actual hours 
 For hospitals, hotels, warehouses and other businesses operating through the night, the repeated hour creates a straightforward timekeeping issue.
 The Labor Department’s example describes an employee scheduled from 11 p.m. to 7:30 a.m., with a 30-minute lunch break. That normally represents eight working hours. During the fall transition, the same schedule produces nine hours because the employee works through the repeated hour. During the spring transition, it produces seven.
 Payroll teams should verify that timekeeping software captures elapsed working time correctly and review overnight records before approving wages.
 The additional hour can also affect overtime. Under federal requirements, covered, nonexempt employees generally must receive at least one-and-a-half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. Working on the clock-change Sunday does not, by itself, create a federal overtime entitlement.
 Energy savings require careful interpretation 
 Energy conservation has long been an argument for daylight saving time. One frequently cited federal finding, however, concerns the extension of the season rather than the entire policy.
 A 2008 Department of Energy analysis estimated that the additional weeks introduced in 2007 saved about 1.3 terawatt-hours of electricity. That represented approximately 0.5 percent of electricity consumption on the extension days, or 0.03 percent of annual U.S. electricity consumption.

 Businesses can make the change easier with a short operational review:

 Check customer appointments, delivery windows and meetings involving locations that do not change clocks.
 Test booking systems and scheduled jobs for the repeated 1 a.m. hour.
 Review evening lighting and worker fatigue procedures.
 Track sales and foot traffic by hour before adjusting staffing or opening times.
 The first payroll review after November 1 will need to account for employees who worked through both occurrences of the 1 a.m. hour. For those workers, the clock will move backward while their paid working time continues.
